title: Newgrounds.com – A community of games, music, and art (newgrounds.com)
comments: I remember playing a crap web game in college, kinda like gunslinger, where you try to shoot people who turn around with a gun (and not those without). title: NTSB Preliminary Report: Prime Air 767 Runway Overrun [pdf] (ntsb.gov)
comments: The captain held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on May 18, 2026. The captain was hired by 21 Air in April 2026. He had accrued about 7,267 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 150 hours were in the accident airplane make and model.The FO held an airline transport pilot certificate with a type rating for the Boeing 767 that he received on April 2, 2025. The FO was hired by 21 Air in February 2025. He had accrued about 2,800 total hours of flight experience, as reported in his interview with NTSB investigators, of which 800 hours were in the accident airplane make and model.This stood out to me --- both pilots are extremely new.reply

For those of you who don't read NTSB reports as a hobby, know that Preliminary reports generally do not assign probable cause or list contributory findings. They're usually just full of basic, factual information like the date, time, location, weather, info about the aircraft and pilot, and so on. So don't go into the PDF thinking you're going to learn the cause of the crash.reply

Should have gone around. Then there was a go-around attempt that came way too late and was aborted.> The landing gear weight-on-wheels (WOW) parameter intermittently switched between “air” to “ground” for about 7 seconds. remaining.> About 4 seconds later, the throttle resolver angles for both engines reduced to idle values at a groundspeed of 117 kts, when wheel brakes were reapplied; the airplane had about 415 ft of runway remaining.reply

> without deploying speed brakes and thrust reverser.I don't think they were able to, since their aircraft never really touched down firmly enough to satisfy the weight-on-wheels interlock system. The aircraft won't allow the crew to reverse thrust until it settles into a "ground state" which we have today because some past guys managed to crash airplanes that way. Also, these guys commanded go-around power when they should have been hitting the brakes, so there's no way the flight systems were going to open the reverser.reply
Indeed, by the time the WOW settled into "ground", they had 2730 ft of runway left. :-/reply

A lot of fallacies and assumptions in this comment.
First of all there is nothing in biology or evolution where the "good of the species" has any kind of bearing on natural selection. This is the group selection hypothesis that has numerous counterexamples. If anything selection happens at the gene level over the long run.There is also no clear reason we know of yet as to why a human being couldn't simply reach sexual maturity and hunting age faster. In fact, there might be at least some evidence other hominids did reach sexual maturity faster. It is not fully understood why humans take so long, but in animal kingdom terms we take roughly as long as the Asian Elephant to reach reproductive maturity. Almost certainly a tradeoff for achieving greater brain development and intelligence, but this could also simply be the consequences of being intelligent (e.g. it's easier to evolve for bigger skulls once ape intelligence surpasses a threshold where the apes are capable of committing to greater early childcare such that natural selection in absence of intelligence is weakened).If dogs were optimized to age and die more quickly for the betterment of the canine species, then you could make the same argument for humanity. That's simply not what's going on. Human ancestors in the past who traded generation time for greater intelligence, likely selfishly outcompeted those who did not, and those other hominids either died off or represent a much smaller allelic contribution to the extant human gene pool.For evolutionary biologists, aging and death similarly likely represent evolutionary tradeoffs. After reaching sexual maturity, as the probability of producing more offspring declines, so too does natural selection as alluded to in the article. Women are born with their entire compliment of ova and the rate of errors increases dramatically as they get older. Men have similar but more subtle issues with sperm generation. These error rate absolutely can be driven by mechanical stresses over time, and I would imagine could be driving much of the selective pressure that puts a cap on human longevity in the long run.reply
